name: Trello
subcategory: team projects, issues and delivery planning
tagline: Run kanban boards with cards, checklists, labels, dates, and simple automation

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Up to 10 collaborators/workspace, 10 boards/workspace, unlimited cards, 10 MB/file and 250 automation runs/month

tiers.name: Standard
tiers.limits: Unlimited boards, 250 MB/file and 1,000 automation runs/month

tiers.name: Premium
tiers.limits: Unlimited automation runs, dashboard/timeline/table/calendar/map views and workspace admin controls

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Unlimited workspaces, organization-wide permissions, public-board controls and Atlassian Guard Standard
tiers.notes: Annual-only starting rate is $210/user/year; per-user price can decrease at higher seat counts.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 10 collaborators/workspace, 10 boards/workspace, unlimited cards, 10 MB/file and 250 automation runs/month
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual for Standard/Premium; Enterprise annual only
pricing.hiddenCosts: Multi-board guests are billed as workspace members. Third-party Power-Ups may charge separate subscriptions. Enterprise uses volume pricing, so the exact per-user rate changes with seat count.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Trello, run kanban boards with cards, checklists, labels, dates, and simple automation. The hard boundary is atlassian ecosystem, power-ups, mobile apps, automation, and reliable collaboration, plus collaboration, integrations, and organizational trust.
coreLoopDIY: Run kanban boards with cards, checklists, labels, dates, and simple automation, and keep comments and a searchable activity history for a small team.
whatYouLose: Atlassian ecosystem, Power-Ups, mobile apps, automation, and reliable collaboration
ongoingBurden: auth, permissions, notifications, search, migrations, audit history, integrations, backups, and uptime
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Trello because teams pay because project state has to remain authoritative through staff changes, outages, and years of accumulated workflow exceptions. The recurring cost buys auth, permissions, notifications, search, migrations, audit history, integrations, backups, and uptime, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Plane
priorArt.desc: Active open-source project and issue tracking platform.

alternatives.name: Wekan
alternatives.desc: Trello's boards without Butler, upsells, or anyone else holding the database

facts.install: Install with Docker Compose or the official Snap package; many other platform packages are community-supported
facts.dataFormat: Boards, cards, users, comments, and settings live in MongoDB; uploaded files and backups must be persisted with the deployment rather than left inside an ephemeral container.
facts.gapVsPaid: Wekan reproduces boards and cards but gives up Trello's Butler automation, Power-Ups, polished mobile apps, integrations, and managed reliability.
facts.setupBlocker: The app starts easily compared with larger suites, but a non-expert still needs an always-on host, persistent MongoDB storage, backups, an external URL, TLS, and mail configuration.

alternatives.name: PLANKA
alternatives.desc: A polished self-hosted Trello clone; the free edition keeps the core board-and-card job intact

facts.install: Hosted PLANKA signup, or the recommended official Docker Compose deployment
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted boards, cards, accounts, and settings live in PostgreSQL; avatars, backgrounds, and attachments are persisted separately and included with the database in PLANKA's backup archive. Hosted data lives with PLANKA.
facts.gapVsPaid: PLANKA is visually close to Trello, but it has no comparable Butler automation or Power-Up ecosystem and its free code is under a restrictive fair-use license rather than an open-source one.
facts.setupBlocker: The free self-hosted Community build still needs Docker Compose, PostgreSQL, a generated secret, base URL, admin creation, persistent storage, TLS, and careful attention to the custom license's permitted-use limits.

alternatives.name: Kanboard
alternatives.desc: Spartan kanban that is finished, not fashionable; maintenance mode means only fixes

facts.install: Docker Compose, or unzip the PHP application into a web server and make its data directory writable
facts.dataFormat: By default all tasks, projects, and users live in one `data/db.sqlite` SQLite file; MariaDB and PostgreSQL are supported, and files/configuration live under the writable data directory.
facts.gapVsPaid: Kanboard is stable and lightweight, but its maintenance-mode pace, dated interface, limited mobile experience, and sparse integrations are a clear downgrade from Trello.
facts.setupBlocker: It is simple by self-hosting standards, but the operator must still secure the default admin account and writable data directory, configure email and backups, and accept that the project is in maintenance mode.

alternatives.name: Taiga
alternatives.desc: Scrum baggage aside, its kanban boards comfortably replace Trello's core job

facts.install: Hosted Taiga signup, or the official multi-container Docker Compose production stack
facts.dataFormat: A self-hosted deployment stores application data in PostgreSQL, messages/events in RabbitMQ, and uploaded media in persistent volumes or configured storage; hosted workspaces live in Taiga's cloud.
facts.gapVsPaid: Taiga's kanban works, but Scrum concepts and project structure make it heavier than Trello while still lacking Trello's automation, Power-Ups, templates, and casual sharing polish.
facts.setupBlocker: Production self-hosting is not one container: it needs Docker/Compose familiarity, several Taiga services, PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, environment files, a reverse proxy, TLS, and email settings.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Focalboard
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Still recommended everywhere; Mattermost stopped maintaining it and the last standalone release was April 2023

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Premium plan and a small-team tracker DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Trello in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: run kanban boards with cards, checklists, labels, dates, and simple automation, and keep comments and a searchable activity history for a small team.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement organizations, projects, members, issues, labels, cycles, and milestones.
Provide list, kanban, and simple timeline views backed by one canonical issue model.
Add comments, mentions, assignments, watchers, and a complete activity log.
Implement project roles for owner, member, and viewer and test every mutation.
Add search, CSV import or export, email notifications, and daily database backups.
Ship Docker Compose, health checks, migrations, seed data, and an admin recovery command.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out hundreds of external integrations.
Deliberately leave out enterprise portfolio planning and SSO.
Deliberately leave out native mobile clients and vendor-operated uptime.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
